terms.lay: Wakes at 4 am, can't sleep again

sayIt.phrase: Dil udaas rehta hai (my heart stays sad)
sayIt.meaning: A steady sadness, described through the heart.
sayIt.why: 'Udaas' is sadness; said of most days it is low mood. Anxious mood would be fear and tension; anhedonia is lost pleasure; irritability is anger.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Low mood

sayIt.phrase: Dil ghabrata hai (my heart feels panicky)
sayIt.meaning: A sudden or constant fearful flutter in the chest.
sayIt.why: 'Ghabrahat' carries fear and a racing heart: anxiety. Rule out heart, thyroid and low sugar before you settle on anxiety, but do not write 'chest pain' as the meaning.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Anxiety symptoms

sayIt.phrase: Kisi kaam mein mann nahi lagta (my mind doesn't settle on any work)
sayIt.meaning: Lost interest and drive for work and hobbies.
sayIt.why: Loss of interest in what used to engage her: anhedonia. Poor concentration is about focus, not interest; apathy and avolition need a different context.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Loss of interest

sayIt.phrase: Raat bhar karvatein badalta rehta hoon (I keep turning all night)
wrong: Early morning awakening with low mood
sayIt.why: Unable to fall and stay asleep: insomnia. Early morning awakening is waking too early and not getting back to sleep; hypersomnia is too much sleep.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Initial and middle insomnia

sayIt.phrase: Sar bhaari bhaari rehta hai (my head stays heavy)
sayIt.meaning: A dull pressure in the head, often with tension or low mood.
sayIt.term: Headache (pressure type), assess for low mood
sayIt.why: A heavy head is a common opening for tension headache and depression. Record it as a pressure headache and ask about mood, sleep and red flags; do not jump to migraine or raised pressure.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Headache (pressure type), assess for low mood

sayIt.phrase: Haath pair thande pad jaate hain (my hands and feet go cold)
sayIt.meaning: Coldness of the limbs, often during fear or panic.
sayIt.why: During fear, blood flow shifts from the limbs: cold hands and feet are autonomic anxiety. Ask when it happens; persistent coldness needs a physical check.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Autonomic anxiety symptoms

sayIt.phrase: Jeene ki ichha nahi rahi (the wish to live is gone)
wrong: Suicidal plan with a chosen method
sayIt.why: A lost wish to live is a passive death wish. It is more than low mood, and not yet a plan. Always ask the next question: any thoughts of ending life?
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Passive death wish

sayIt.phrase: Tension hai, bahut tension (there is tension, a lot)
sayIt.meaning: General stress, worry or bodily tightness.
sayIt.why: 'Tension' in Indian English can mean worry, stress, a headache or even low mood. Write the patient's word, then clarify: it is not hypertension or a diagnosis by itself.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Stress or anxiety

sayIt.phrase: Pet mein gas banti hai, upar chadhti hai (gas forms in the stomach and rises up)
sayIt.meaning: Bloating or chest discomfort, often with anxiety or low mood.
sayIt.term: Somatic complaint: abdominal bloating or chest discomfort
sayIt.why: 'Gas' is the commonest body word for distress in Indian clinics. Record the complaint plainly, check physical causes, and screen for anxiety and depression. It is not a delusion.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Somatic complaint: abdominal bloating or chest discomfort

sayIt.phrase: Kamzori lagti hai, haath pair mein jaan nahi (weakness, no life in my arms and legs)
sayIt.why: Generalised weakness in Indian speech usually means tiredness: anergia. True muscle weakness is a neurological sign and needs examination.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Fatigue and low energy

sayIt.phrase: Kisi ne jaadu tona kar diya hai (someone has done black magic)
sayIt.meaning: A cultural explanation for illness or misfortune.
sayIt.why: Belief in sorcery is shared in many communities; record it as the explanatory model. It becomes a delusion only if it is fixed, idiosyncratic and out of keeping with the family's own beliefs.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Patient's explanatory model: sorcery

sayIt.phrase: Chhoti chhoti baat pe gussa aa jaata hai (I get angry at small things)
sayIt.why: Anger at small things: irritability, seen in depression, anxiety, mania and stress. Hostility is directed threat; mania is a diagnosis.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Irritability

sayIt.phrase: Bhookh mar gayi hai (hunger has died)
sayIt.why: Loss of appetite. Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder with a fear of weight gain, not just poor appetite.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Reduced appetite

sayIt.phrase: Sab kuch bekaar lagta hai, koi faayda nahi (everything feels useless, no point)
sayIt.why: 'No point in anything' is hopelessness, a strong suicide risk marker. A nihilistic delusion is a fixed belief that things are dead or gone.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Hopelessness

sayIt.phrase: Kuch yaad nahi rehta (nothing stays in memory)
sayIt.why: Record it as a complaint and test it. Depression and anxiety often cause this through poor attention; dementia is a diagnosis made after testing.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Subjective memory complaint

sayIt.phrase: Mere dimaag mein koi aur soch daal raha hai (someone else is putting thoughts in my mind)
sayIt.why: Thoughts felt as not one's own and placed from outside: insertion. In an obsession the person knows the thought is their own.
sayIt.objective: Tell Thought insertion from Obsessional thought

sayIt.phrase: Log meri soch sun lete hain (people can hear my thoughts)
sayIt.meaning: Others know his thoughts as they happen.
sayIt.why: Others know his thoughts: broadcasting. Thought echo is the patient himself hearing his thoughts aloud.
sayIt.objective: Tell Thought broadcasting from Thought echo

sayIt.phrase: Kaan mein awaazein aati hain (voices come in my ears)
sayIt.why: Voices heard through the ears with no speaker: auditory hallucinations. Ask whether they feel inside or outside the head, and whether there was a real sound.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Auditory hallucinations

sayIt.phrase: Neend ki zaroorat hi nahi, phir bhi taaza hoon (no need for sleep, still fresh)
sayIt.why: Sleeping little but feeling rested is decreased need for sleep, a key manic sign. In insomnia the person wants sleep and feels tired.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Decreased need for sleep

sayIt.phrase: Seene mein jalan aur bhaaripan (burning and heaviness in the chest)
sayIt.meaning: Chest discomfort, sometimes anxiety or reflux.
sayIt.term: Chest discomfort, rule out cardiac and gastric causes
sayIt.why: Chest symptoms need a physical check first. Then screen for anxiety and depression. Never write 'panic' as the meaning of chest pain.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Chest discomfort, rule out cardiac and gastric causes

sayIt.phrase: Peshaab mein dhaat jaati hai, isliye kamzori hai (semen goes in urine, that's why I'm weak)
sayIt.meaning: A cultural belief that semen loss causes weakness.
sayIt.why: Dhat is a culture-related syndrome: anxiety and low mood attributed to semen loss. It is a shared belief, not a delusion. Screen for depression and anxiety and educate gently.
sayIt.objective: Tell Dhat syndrome from Somatic delusion

sayIt.phrase: Padhai mein dhyaan nahi lagta (can't focus on studies)
sayIt.why: Difficulty focusing: poor concentration. Learning disability and intellectual level need testing, not assumption.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Poor concentration

sayIt.phrase: Main sab pe bojh hoon (I am a burden on everyone)
sayIt.why: Feeling a burden is a known suicide risk factor. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts. It is not a delusion unless fixed and bizarre.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Perceived burdensomeness

sayIt.phrase: Haath kaanpte hain (my hands shake)
sayIt.why: Shaking hands: tremor. Ask when it happens, with anxiety, alcohol, lithium or thyroid.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Tremor

sayIt.phrase: Mata aati hai (the goddess comes)
sayIt.meaning: A trance or possession state, often accepted in the community.
sayIt.why: Possession in a community that accepts it is not illness by itself. It becomes a disorder when unwanted, distressing or impairing. Rule out seizures.
sayIt.objective: Tell Possession trance from Psychotic episode

sayIt.phrase: Rona aata hai bina baat ke (I cry for no reason)
sayIt.why: Crying for no reason is tearfulness, a low mood sign. Labile affect is rapid swings in the room; pseudobulbar affect follows brain injury.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Tearfulness

sayIt.phrase: Har waqt darr lagta hai kuch bura hoga (always afraid something bad will happen)
sayIt.why: A general sense of dread not tied to one object: free-floating anxiety. A phobia is fear of a specific thing.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Free-floating anxiety

sayIt.phrase: Mere haath mera nahi, koi aur chala raha hai (my hand is not mine, someone else moves it)
sayIt.meaning: Movements controlled by an outside force.
sayIt.why: Belief that an outside force moves his hand: made actions, a first-rank symptom. In depersonalisation he would know it is his own hand, only feeling unreal. Alien hand syndrome is neurological, without the belief.
sayIt.objective: Write the full clinical description: Passivity of volition

sayIt.phrase: Subah 4 baje aankh khul jaati hai (my eyes open at 4 am)
sayIt.meaning: Wakes early and can't sleep again.
sayIt.why: Waking hours early, unable to sleep again: early morning awakening, a depressive sign.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Early morning awakening

sayIt.phrase: Poore badan mein dard (pain all over the body)
sayIt.why: Widespread pain: record it plainly, screen physically and for depression. Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis, not a translation.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Generalised body ache

sayIt.phrase: Unki awaaz sunai deti hai kabhi kabhi (I sometimes hear his voice)
sayIt.meaning: Hearing a dead spouse's voice briefly.
sayIt.why: Brief voices of the dead in grief are common and usually not psychosis, especially with insight. Note frequency and distress.
sayIt.objective: Tell Bereavement hallucination from Schizophrenia with voices

sayIt.phrase: Mera dimaag bahut tez chal raha hai (my brain is running very fast)
sayIt.why: Racing thoughts are what he feels; flight of ideas is what you hear in his speech. Write both if present.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Racing thoughts

sayIt.phrase: Mar jaana chahta hoon (I want to die)
sayIt.why: A direct wish to die: suicidal ideation. Ask about plan, intent and means. 'Attention seeking' is a stigmatising word, not a clinical term.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Suicidal ideation

sayIt.phrase: TV wale mere baare mein baat karte hain (people on TV talk about me)
sayIt.meaning: Belief that TV refers to him.
sayIt.why: Belief that the TV talks about him: reference. If he can doubt it, it is an idea of reference; if fixed, a delusion.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Delusion of reference

sayIt.phrase: Andar se khokhla ho gaya hoon, kuch mehsoos nahi hota (I've become hollow inside, I feel nothing)
sayIt.meaning: Painful emptiness and loss of feeling.
sayIt.why: Painful inability to feel, reported by the person: loss of feeling, seen in severe depression. Flat affect is what you observe; nihilism is a fixed belief of being dead.
sayIt.objective: Write the full clinical description: Loss of feeling

sayIt.phrase: Saans phoolti hai (my breath swells, breathless)
sayIt.why: Record breathlessness, then look for the cause: lungs, heart, anaemia or panic. Do not write the diagnosis as the meaning.
sayIt.objective: Recognise the phrase as Breathlessness

sayIt.phrase: Baat karte karte bhool jaata hoon kya keh raha tha (I forget mid-sentence what I was saying)
sayIt.why: This needs a closer look: in anxiety it is poor attention; in psychosis it may be thought block. Ask what the mind feels like at that moment.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Losing the thread
sayIt.note: check for thought block or poor attention

sayIt.phrase: Nas mein khinchaav hai (the nerves are pulling)
sayIt.meaning: A pulling or tight feeling, often attributed to nerves.
sayIt.why: 'Nas' language is a common body idiom of stress. Examine, then record the feeling plainly.
sayIt.objective: Turn the patient's words into Somatic tension complaint

sayIt.phrase: Main paapi hoon, mujhe saza milni chahiye (I am a sinner, I should be punished)
sayIt.why: Ask how fixed it is. A fixed, far-out-of-proportion belief of sin deserving punishment, in depression, is a delusion of guilt, with high suicide risk.
sayIt.objective: Tell Delusion of guilt from Normal religious belief
sayIt.note: if fixed and out of proportion

sayIt.phrase: Subah thoda peeta hoon toh haath nahi kaanpte (a little in the morning stops my hands shaking)
sayIt.meaning: Drinking in the morning to relieve tremor.
sayIt.why: Drinking to relieve withdrawal tremor in the morning is relief drinking, a dependence sign. Tolerance is needing more for the same effect.
sayIt.objective: Recall the case-sheet term: Relief drinking

scenarios.objective: Ask about suicide directly and act the same day

beats.says: “Honestly, nothing matters anymore. Everyone would be fine without me.”

choices.text: “It sounds like things feel really heavy. Are you having thoughts of ending your life?”
choices.consequence: She pauses, then says yes, sometimes at night. You now know what you're dealing with.

choices.text: “Don't say that! Your family loves you.”
choices.consequence: She feels dismissed and says “forget it”. The risk is still there, and now it's hidden.

choices.text: “Let's focus on your studies first, then we'll talk feelings.”
choices.consequence: You get exam details, but you've skipped the most important question.

beats.says: “Sometimes I think about taking all my mother's sleeping pills.”
beats.context: She has access to the pills. No previous attempt.

choices.text: Ask about intent and timing, make a safety plan, and involve your supervisor today
choices.consequence: She agrees to her mother keeping the pills and to a follow-up tomorrow. Your supervisor reviews her the same day.

choices.text: Promise to keep it between the two of you so she trusts you
choices.consequence: You've made a promise you can't keep. If she's at risk, you must act, and she'll feel betrayed.

choices.text: Book her next weekly session as usual
choices.consequence: She's still at risk for 7 days with access to the means. Risk needs same-day action.

scenarios.objective: Spot mania and an antidepressant trigger

beats.says: “I haven't slept in 4 days and I've never felt better! I'm launching three companies.”

choices.text: Ask about sleep, spending, risky decisions and past depressions
choices.consequence: You learn she spent ₹2 lakh this week and had a long depression last year. Mania is likely.

choices.text: “That's amazing, you're so motivated!”
choices.consequence: You've reinforced the grandiosity and missed a probable manic episode.

choices.text: Suggest a sleep hygiene sheet
choices.consequence: Sleep matters, but this needs a psychiatric review, not a handout.

beats.says: “My GP gave me an antidepressant last month for low mood.”

choices.text: Flag it urgently to the psychiatrist: an antidepressant alone may have triggered mania
choices.consequence: The psychiatrist reviews her the same day and changes the plan.

choices.text: Tell her to stop the tablet today
choices.consequence: Medicine changes are the prescriber's job. Stopping suddenly can cause other problems.

choices.text: Note it and move on
choices.consequence: It's documented, but a key safety issue wasn't escalated.

scenarios.objective: Respond to delusions without arguing or agreeing, then assess command voices

beats.says: “The voices say you're working with my neighbours. Are you recording me?”

choices.text: “I'm not recording you. It sounds frightening to feel watched. Can you tell me about the voices?”
choices.consequence: He relaxes slightly and describes two voices commenting on him.

choices.text: “There are no voices. That's just your illness talking.”
choices.consequence: Arguing with a delusion breaks trust. He stops talking.

choices.text: “Okay, yes, let's say the neighbours are involved.”
choices.consequence: Agreeing with the delusion reinforces it and isn't honest.

beats.says: “The voices tell me to hurt the neighbour's dog.”

choices.text: Ask if he plans to act, whether he's acted before, and inform the psychiatrist today
choices.consequence: Command hallucinations with possible action need urgent review. The team acts in time.

choices.text: Reassure him that voices can't make him do anything
choices.consequence: Kind, but you haven't assessed the risk.

choices.text: Change the topic to keep him calm
choices.consequence: You've avoided a risk you were told about.

beats.says: “Can you just tell me my hands are clean? Please, just say it once.”

choices.text: Gently explain that reassurance feeds OCD, and stay with her anxiety together
choices.consequence: Her anxiety rises, then slowly settles. She's learning it passes without the ritual.

choices.text: “Yes, your hands are clean.”
choices.consequence: Instant relief, then she asks again in 5 minutes. Reassurance works like a compulsion.

choices.text: Ignore the question
choices.consequence: No reassurance given, but she feels unheard. Explain why instead.

words.why: 'Committed' suggests a crime. Suicide is a health outcome.
Person-first: the illness isn't their identity.

words.better: the account is inconsistent with collateral
seeking connection / help in a risky way
words.why: The behaviour is a signal of need; labels shut down curiosity.

words.better: not taking the medicine as prescribed (reasons explored)
words.why: Invites the 'why': side effects, cost, beliefs.

words.better: person with a substance use disorder
words.why: Reduces stigma and treats it as a health condition.
'Failed' implies death was a goal to succeed at.

clinics.objective: Look past body complaints to the depressive core
clues: Eight months of body ache and heaviness
clinics.line: A 34-year-old man, 8 months of body ache, 'heaviness', broken sleep, 6kg weight loss. Three GP visits for 'gas' and 'weakness'.
clinics.expertNext: Ask about sleep, appetite, anhedonia, then screen for suicidal ideation directly.
clinics.lesson: Somatic-first depression is the most common missed presentation in Indian primary care. Never accept 'gas' without asking about sleep and mood.

clinics.objective: Recognise panic after normal cardiac work-ups
clues: Palpitations and fear of dying on the metro
Three emergency visits, every cardiac test normal
Four months of attacks with growing worry about the next one
clinics.line: A 28-year-old woman, 4 months of palpitations and fear of dying on the metro. 3 ER visits, all cardiac workups normal.
clinics.expertNext: Ask about anticipatory anxiety and avoidance: has she stopped doing things to avoid the sensation?
clinics.lesson: Normal cardiac workup + fear of dying + avoidance = panic until proven otherwise.

clues: Eight months after his wife died
Talks to her chair, sorts her clothes slowly
Daughter worried he is 'not moving on'
clinics.line: A 60-year-old retired teacher, 8 months after his wife died, talks to her chair and sorts her clothes one drawer a week. Daughter worried he's 'not moving on'.
clinics.expertNext: Check for preserved pleasure (grandchildren?), sleep, appetite, and whether the grief has 'waves'.
clinics.lesson: Preserved pleasure with waves of grief = normal grief. Over-diagnosing this is the error.

clinics.objective: Unpack a vague idiom before interpreting it
clues: In Indian English this often means bowels or unrefreshing sleep
clinics.diagnosis: Undefined complaint: 'not feeling fresh' needs instantiation
clinics.expertNext: "When you say fresh: what would feeling fresh look like? Walk me through yesterday morning from waking up."
clinics.lesson: "Not feeling fresh" is the classic idiom, in Indian English it often means constipation. The funnel's instantiate step is the highest-yield question.

scenarios.vignette: A 22-year-old student tells you, in session 2, that she has a specific plan to end her life tonight and the means. She asks you not to tell anyone.

options.label: Continue and keep her confidence: breaking it would damage trust.
Continue but mention it to a supervisor.
Activate the safety plan now: emergency referral, involve support, do not leave her alone.
Ask her to get a full medical check first.

scenarios.reasoning: A specific plan + means + intent tonight is imminent risk. Confidentiality has limits; emergency action overrides it. You stay with her until handover.

scenarios.vignette: A client says he's been 'hearing a voice telling me to hurt people' for two weeks, and yesterday he almost acted on it. He's never seen anyone before you.

options.label: Continue. It's probably stress, and you're building rapport.
Continue but log it with a supervisor.
Urgent referral: command hallucinations with action risk need immediate psychiatric assessment.
Rule out a medical cause first with a GP.

scenarios.reasoning: Command hallucinations with near-action is a psychiatric emergency. Not your call to hold.

scenarios.vignette: A client on an SSRI from a GP says she's been feeling 'amazing, unstoppable, sleeping 3 hours' for two weeks, after being treated for depression for a year.

options.label: Celebrate. She's clearly better.
Note the improvement and keep going.
Suspect antidepressant-induced hypomania: refer to a psychiatrist who can review the medication.
Send for a thyroid panel first.

scenarios.reasoning: New euphoric highs in a depressed patient on an SSRI is hypomania until proven otherwise: the medication itself may be driving it, and only a prescriber can change it.

dilemmas.vignette: During a hospital visit to see a client, you find them in a locked side-room alone for 'their safety'. The staff say it's been six hours.

options.label: Accept it: hospitals know what they're doing.
options.consequence: Six hours of seclusion without documented review is a likely MHA violation you've witnessed and ignored.

options.label: Compromise: mention your concern to the client afterwards so they can complain.
options.consequence: You chose a half-measure. It feels safer than either extreme, but it is the choice that satisfies no one and protects no one. The middle path here is where the real damage happens: not the worst act, but the one that looks reasonable until it is examined.

options.label: Document what you saw, raise it with the treating team and the hospital's grievance channel, and support the client afterwards.
options.consequence: Correct. Seclusion has strict limits and documentation duties under MHA 2017; silence is complicity.

dilemmas.law: MHA 2017: seclusion and restraint are last-resort, time-limited, and must be documented and reported.

dilemmas.vignette: You want to record sessions for supervision. The client hesitates but eventually says 'fine' when you push a little.

options.label: Record. They said fine.
options.consequence: That 'fine' is not informed consent; it's pressure-induced compliance. The recording has no ethical basis.

options.label: Compromise: record but promise to delete it right after supervision.
options.consequence: You chose a half-measure. It feels safer than either extreme, but it is the choice that satisfies no one and protects no one. The middle path here is where the real damage happens: not the worst act, but the one that looks reasonable until it is examined.

options.label: Explain what the recording is for, who will hear it, how it's stored and deleted, and treat a 'fine' under pressure as a no.
options.consequence: Correct. Informed consent is specific, voluntary, and revocable. You document the explanation and the agreement.

dilemmas.law: RCI code of ethics: informed consent for recording; pressure-induced compliance is not consent.

dilemmas.vignette: A client is being discharged from a psychiatric unit after 3 weeks. Their family says the doctors 'didn't tell us anything about the medicine' and the client is confused about what they're taking.

options.label: It's the hospital's job. Nothing to do with you.
options.consequence: You've missed a transition moment where relapse is likeliest. Discharge without understanding is a failed handover.

options.label: Compromise: tell the family to ask the pharmacy about the medicines.
options.consequence: You chose a half-measure. It feels safer than either extreme, but it is the choice that satisfies no one and protects no one. The middle path here is where the real damage happens: not the worst act, but the one that looks reasonable until it is examined.

options.label: Help them make a written medication/support plan for discharge, and flag the information gap to the treating team for a proper handover.
options.consequence: Correct. Discharge planning is part of continuity of care; a confused patient leaving with medicines they don't understand is a foreseeable harm.

dilemmas.law: MHA 2017: continuity of care and informed consent for treatment, including medication information.

quiz.prompt: A 14-year-old tells you a relative has been touching her. Would you report?
options: Yes: POCSO mandates reporting to police/Childline, no discretion
Only if she confirms it a second time
quiz.rationale: POCSO Section 19 imposes a mandatory reporting duty; failure is itself an offence.

quiz.prompt: A client's advance directive refuses ECT. The family demands it. Which is standard of care?
options: Honour the directive and use the MHA's review mechanism if overriding is considered (standard)
Follow the family's wishes as the 'real' decision-makers (common but wrong)
quiz.rationale: MHA 2017 Section 5 makes advance directives binding; exceptions are narrow and must be invoked.

quiz.prompt: Order the correct steps when a client discloses imminent risk of harm to another person.
options: Explore the plan → involve authorities/support → document the confidentiality break
Document first → then explore the plan
Tell the family first → then decide
Wait for the session to end naturally
quiz.rationale: Assess the immediacy and plan, act on the identified risk, then document the proportionate confidentiality break.
quiz.source: RCI code of ethics: limits of confidentiality

spots.teachCard: Reflection vs reassurance: the card that names the difference

spots.teachCard: When confidentiality is absolute, and when it is breached

spots.label: Premature reassurance
spots.teachCard: Why premature reassurance is the #1 novice error

spots.remedyLabel: Consulting Room: aim for open questions

drill.scenario: A patient says 'Everyone at home just treats me like a machine.'
drill.strongLine: 'Treated like a machine, like your feelings aren't part of the arrangement?'
drill.why: A generic 'stressful' reflects nothing; echoing the exact phrase shows you heard the person.

drill.scenario: A patient says 'I don't even know why I came.'
drill.weakLine: 'Well, you came because your family brought you.'
drill.strongLine: 'You're not sure this is the right place: what would make it worth being here?'
drill.why: Correcting the patient closes the door; reflecting the uncertainty keeps it open.

drill.scenario: A patient pauses a long time, then says '…It's nothing.'
drill.weakLine: 'Okay, so moving on: any other symptoms?'
drill.strongLine: 'That pause said something before the words did. I'm in no hurry.'
drill.why: The pause is the content; a reflection that names it earns the disclosure.

drill.scenario: The patient has been opening up well for ten minutes. You haven't asked about self-harm.
drill.weakLine: 'Let's wait, maybe next session if it feels right.'
drill.strongLine: 'After everything you've shared: have you had thoughts of ending your life?'
drill.why: Risk asked in clear language at rapport height earns a true answer; delayed risk assessment is the classic miss.

drill.scenario: The patient mentions 'not wanting to be here' in passing.
drill.weakLine: 'You mentioned not wanting to be here: do you mean this session?'
drill.strongLine: 'When you say not wanting to be here: do you mean here in the room, or here in life?'
drill.why: The ambiguous 'here' is a risk moment; asking it clearly costs nothing and can find everything.

drill.scenario: A patient says 'I'm scared I'm losing my mind.'
drill.weakLine: 'Don't worry, you're definitely not losing your mind!'
drill.strongLine: 'That's a frightening fear to carry. What makes you feel you're losing your mind?'
drill.why: Reassurance before exploration tells the patient you can't hold their distress: exploring first is the reassurance that works.

drill.scenario: A patient says 'I think about dying a lot.'
drill.weakLine: 'You'll be fine, these thoughts are normal.'
drill.strongLine: 'That's important: thank you for telling me. When you say dying, what exactly have you been thinking?'
drill.why: Rushing to normalise a risk disclosure teaches the patient not to share; taking it seriously keeps them safe and talking.

drill.scenario: A patient says 'I can't cope with anything anymore.'
drill.weakLine: 'Everyone feels that way sometimes, you're doing great!'
drill.strongLine: 'It sounds like things feel like too much right now. What's the heaviest part?'
drill.why: Cheerleading invalidates; sitting with the heaviness is the therapeutic act.

drill.scenario: A patient says 'I'm not feeling fresh.'
drill.strongLine: 'When you say fresh: what does that look like for you?'
drill.why: Closed questions close exploration; the open version finds the meaning (constipation, sleep, mood).

drill.strongLine: 'What's that been like at home lately?'
drill.why: Guessing the referent wastes the question; open invites the actual story.

observe.content: A 19-year-old student sits in the chair across from you, arms crossed, wearing yesterday's shirt. She glances at the door twice in the first minute. When she speaks her voice is barely audible and she uses exactly eight words per answer. Her hands are clasped so tight her knuckles are white. After you ask about sleep, she is silent for eleven seconds before saying 'fine.'
observe.objective: Describe what you see and hear, with no labels

observe.content: A 52-year-old shopkeeper sits slumped, shoulders rolled forward, in a checked shirt that is clean but crumpled. He runs his palm across his eyes every few seconds as if tired. His speech is slow, soft, and he lets sentences trail off and restart. When the shop is mentioned, he leans forward slightly and begins to shake his foot. He maintains eye contact only when discussing business.
observe.objective: Describe what you see and hear, with no labels

observe.content: A 40-year-old woman is brought in by her sister. She sits very still, hands folded in her lap, and does not speak first. Her sari is neat. When she finally speaks it is in a flat, even voice, and she looks at her sister before every answer. Twice, when the sister begins to answer for her, she closes her eyes for several seconds. She is the only one in the room who has not shifted posture once.
observe.objective: Describe what you see and hear, with no labels

observe.content: A 26-year-old man paces the small consulting room, pausing only to glance at the clock. He sits, immediately stands, then sits again. His voice is loud and rapid, and he finishes his sentences in bursts, hands gesturing. He laughs when he describes a fight with his landlord, though nothing in the story is funny. When asked to slow down, he apologises, taps his foot continuously, and returns to the same speed within twenty seconds.
observe.objective: Describe what you see and hear, with no labels

domain.content: A 45-year-old clerk arrives with three days of stubble, a shirt stained at the collar and hair uncombed. His wife says he used to iron his clothes every morning.
domain.why: Unwashed and uncared-for compared with his usual standard is unkempt. Dishevelled is close (untidy, disordered) and fair as a second word.

domain.content: A 30-year-old teacher in a pressed cotton sari, hair neatly tied, sits upright and smiles as she greets you.
domain.why: Clean, neat and dressed for her age and setting: well-groomed and age-appropriate. A normal appearance line is still written.

domain.content: A 16-year-old girl wears a loose hoodie in summer. Her cheekbones are prominent, wrists bony, and her mother says she has lost 9 kg in four months.
domain.why: Visible thinness with recent weight loss is the key appearance finding: underweight. The loose clothes hide it, which is why you look at wrists and face.

domain.content: A 28-year-old man in a gold sequinned jacket, red sunglasses indoors, three chains and bright lipstick on one cheek, at 10 am in the OPD.
domain.why: Bright, showy clothes beyond the setting, typical of mania: flamboyant dress. Bizarre dress is odd for a private reason (foil hat) rather than showy.
domain.objective: Name the appearance finding: flamboyant dress

domain.content: A 33-year-old man wears a woollen cap lined with kitchen foil and two sweaters on a hot afternoon. He says the foil stops the signals.
domain.why: Clothing strikingly out of place for a delusional reason: bizarre dress. Whether he is also unkempt depends on hygiene, which is not described.
domain.objective: Tag appearance without sliding into another domain

domain.content: When a 19-year-old student rolls up her sleeve for a BP check, there are rows of thin, healed and fresh cuts on her left forearm.
domain.why: Healed and fresh cuts at different stages: visible self-harm scars. Record them neutrally and ask about them kindly in private.
domain.objective: Name the appearance finding: visible self-harm scars

domain.content: A 50-year-old man has a red, puffy face, small red spider-like veins on his cheeks, a tremor of the hands and smells strongly of alcohol at noon.
domain.why: The smell of alcohol at noon is a sign of current intoxication; his weathered face makes him look older than 50. Tremor belongs in behaviour.
domain.objective: Tag appearance without sliding into another domain

domain.content: An 82-year-old widow is neatly dressed by her daughter, hair oiled and plaited, a fresh bindi.
domain.why: Clean and neat: well-groomed. Note who maintains grooming if relevant. Well-groomed means clean and neatly kept for the setting. Age-appropriate (dressed and presented in keeping with age and culture) is only a partial fit here.

domain.content: A 40-year-old labourer wears an old, torn but clean vest and washed lungi. He has walked 12 km to the clinic.
domain.why: Old, worn but clean clothes reflect poverty, not self-neglect. Do not call him unkempt: unkempt means unwashed and uncared for compared with his own standard.

domain.content: A 38-year-old man in a long-stay ward has matted hair, long dirty nails and a strong body odour. Staff say he refuses baths.
domain.why: Neglect of hygiene: unkempt and dishevelled. In chronic psychosis this often reflects negative symptoms. Unkempt means unwashed or uncared for compared with the person's usual standard.
domain.objective: Tag appearance without sliding into another domain

fullMse.title: Sandeep, 35: the man who can't sit in a meeting
fullMse.context: A 35-year-old accountant, brought by his wife. Six weeks ago a colleague teased him about 'losing focus'. Since then he has been pacing the office, snapping at people, and taking 'walks' that last an hour. Tonight he sat rigidly until the clinic door closed, then began shaking and said: 'I can't sit still. It's like my legs decide, not me.' He is on an antipsychotic started by a GP for 'tension'.

thought_content: insight into restlessness but not cause
insight: describes the restlessness as 'my legs decide': externalised
judgment: poor when describing the snapping at colleagues
small_things: rigid until the door closed, then shaking: the controlled exterior dropped at privacy
said his legs decide, not him: externalised agency

smallThings.moment: The patient made eye contact the whole session, until you asked about the marriage.
smallThings.read: A topic-specific avoidance pattern, not general shyness.
smallThings.move: Seed the topic again later, more gently, and watch whether the same thing recurs.

smallThings.moment: The patient's leg was tapping constantly. It stopped the moment the marriage was mentioned.
smallThings.read: Either the topic is charged, or it's relief it finally came up.
smallThings.move: Wait in the silence: the pause after a topic change is often where they either shut or open.

smallThings.moment: You asked about sleep. The patient answered a different question, about work.
smallThings.read: Answering the wrong question is a deflection with a direction; the avoided topic is the topic.
smallThings.move: Reflect it: 'I noticed when I asked about sleep you brought up work, what is that about?'

smallThings.moment: The patient described a recent event in the past tense about themselves: 'I was a good father.'
smallThings.read: The past tense about the self can signal the person no longer identifies with who they were.
smallThings.move: Gently explore: 'You said you WERE a good father, how do you see yourself now?'

smallThings.moment: Before answering, the patient looked at the family member who brought them.
smallThings.read: Permission-seeking: the disclosure has family consequences.
smallThings.move: Separate the patient from the family for at least part of the session; name the dynamic directly.

smallThings.moment: You asked the risk question. There was a long pause before the patient said 'no.'
smallThings.read: The pause is the disclosure. A practised 'no' comes fast; a real one hesitates or shifts.
smallThings.move: Follow the pause: 'You took a moment before no, what was in it?'

smallThings.moment: The patient's speech was steady and slow, then sped up markedly when the topic changed to the exam.
smallThings.read: Rate change is an arousal marker; the accelerated topic is charged.
smallThings.move: Return to the slower register to understand what the speed is protecting.

smallThings.moment: The patient is wearing the same clothes described at the last visit, and they're not clean.
smallThings.read: Self-care decline across sessions: a functional marker, not just appearance.
smallThings.move: Check the pattern: 'In the last two weeks, how many days have you showered?'

smallThings.moment: The patient laughed at something that was not funny.
smallThings.read: Incongruent affect: the laugh is doing work (deflection, masking, or frank incongruity).
smallThings.move: Name it lightly and watch whether the affect broadens or stays flat.

smallThings.moment: The patient said 'we decided' about a decision that was clearly theirs alone.
smallThings.read: The 'we' can signal enmeshment, a dominating family, or a lack of ownership over their own life.
smallThings.move: Clarify who 'we' is, and whose decision it truly was.

smallThings.moment: The patient shifted posture, uncrossed arms and leaned forward, right after you validated them.
smallThings.read: Validation caused an approach response; the patient is opening.
smallThings.move: Continue on the validation, now gently deepen the topic it opened.

smallThings.moment: The patient's voice went quiet and the sentence dropped off before it finished.
smallThings.read: Trailing off often precedes the hard thing: the mouth stops before the mind decides.
smallThings.move: Let the silence hold; do not rescue it. Then reflect what you saw.

smallThings.moment: You offered a referral or a clinic; the patient immediately asked how much it costs.
smallThings.read: Cost is the gate for disclosure. Answer it plainly and the door opens.
smallThings.move: Address cost directly and early. It is a presenting problem, not a distraction.

smallThings.moment: The patient answered everything, then asked you one question about yourself.
smallThings.read: A question back is the patient testing whether you are safe to trust.
smallThings.move: Answer honestly and briefly, then return to them. Do not sidestep it.

smallThings.moment: The patient keeps checking their phone every time a notification pings, even mid-answer.
smallThings.read: Sustained attention to the phone during the session is avoidance with a prop, or a self-soothing tic under anxiety.
smallThings.move: Name it without accusation: 'I notice your phone keeps pulling at you, would it help to put it aside for this hour?'

smallThings.moment: Every answer is 'yes' or 'no' with no elaboration, but the patient is clearly not upset. They just will not volunteer.
smallThings.read: Total compliance with no content is not engagement; it is the patient waiting for permission to stop.
smallThings.move: Ask for their opinion, not their status: 'What do YOU make of what the doctor said?'

smallThings.moment: The patient walked in wearing headphones and took them off only when you asked.
smallThings.read: The headphones are a boundary: the patient is signalling reluctance to engage, not rudeness.
smallThings.move: Honour the boundary first: 'Thanks for taking those off. We can put them back on anytime.'

smallThings.moment: The patient's hands are in their lap, perfectly still, even when describing the panic attacks.
smallThings.read: Stillness during panic content is over-control; the body is being held rigidly against the subject.
smallThings.move: Watch for micro-movements when you probe the panic: the release of tension is data.

smallThings.moment: When you summarised the session, the patient corrected a word you used about their situation.
smallThings.read: The correction is ownership: the patient is claiming the narrative and telling you what matters to them.
smallThings.move: Adopt their word and check what difference it makes: 'You said 'struggle', not 'depression', what is the difference to you?'

smallThings.moment: The patient answered about their father's death fluently, but the hands began trembling mid-answer.
smallThings.read: The voice can deliver a rehearsed story while the body tells the unprocessed one.
smallThings.move: Slow down: 'Your hands are shaking a little, is that how it feels inside?'

items.vignette: A 24-year-old woman comes in with 2 months of poor sleep, low energy, and tearfulness. She says she's 'just stressed' about work.
items.new_information: Her appetite has increased and she has gained 4 kg. She sleeps 12+ hours on weekends.

items.vignette: A 30-year-old man reports palpitations, sweating, and fear of dying that started 3 months ago on the metro. Cardiac workup was normal.
items.new_information: He now avoids buses and crowds, and has stopped going to the gym because 'the heart thing' might happen there.

items.vignette: A 19-year-old student has intrusive blasphemous thoughts and washes his hands 30 times a day. He is ashamed and thinks he's 'possessed'.
items.new_information: He has missed 11 days of college this semester because of the washing rituals.

items.vignette: A 45-year-old businessman is brought by his wife for 'drinking too much'. He denies it and says business stress is the issue.
items.new_information: He drives home from work after drinking most evenings.

items.vignette: A 26-year-old woman, 6 months postpartum, says she's 'not a good mother' and cries daily. Her mother-in-law does most of the childcare.
items.new_information: She has had thoughts of 'the baby would be better off without me': passive, no plan.

cases.title: Phineas Gage
cases.story: In 1848, a railway foreman survived an iron rod through his frontal lobes. His friends said 'Gage was no longer Gage': the polite, reliable man became impulsive and profane.
cases.believedThen: That personality lived in a single 'seat', and that the accident proved it was the front of the brain.
cases.understandNow: The frontal lobes modulate behaviour, but personality is distributed. Gage is the origin story of 'executive function', and later accounts note his social recovery was better than the myth claimed.

quiz.question: What is Gage's lasting lesson?
options: The frontal lobes modulate impulse and social behaviour
quiz.rationale: Gage demonstrated that frontal damage changes social-emotional regulation: the founding case of executive function.

quiz.question: Why is the 'Gage was no longer Gage' account now qualified?
options: It was invented by the press
Later evidence shows significant social recovery, complicating the myth
quiz.rationale: Modern re-analysis suggests his functioning recovered more than the legend, teaching students to read famous cases critically.

quiz.question: What domain does Gage belong to?
quiz.rationale: Gage is a neuropsychology landmark: brain-behaviour mapping.

tags.objective: Link frontal lobe damage to changes in behaviour

cases.title: H.M. (Henry Molaison)
cases.story: To stop severe epilepsy, Molaison had both medial temporal lobes removed in 1953. The epilepsy improved. He could no longer form new memories: his life froze at the operation.
cases.believedThen: Memory was a single faculty; the brain didn't 'store' experiences in a way an operation could destroy.
cases.understandNow: H.M. revealed the distinction between declarative memory (what, gone for him) and procedural memory (how, intact). He could learn a mirror-tracing task and deny ever having seen it. That split is still the backbone of memory science.

quiz.question: H.M. taught us that memory is:
options: Divided into declarative and procedural systems
quiz.rationale: H.M.'s intact procedural learning alongside lost declarative memory proved memory is multiple systems.

quiz.question: Which task could H.M. learn despite his amnesia?
quiz.rationale: Procedural (skill) memory survived; declarative did not: mirror-tracing is a skill.

tags.objective: Explain the split between declarative and procedural memory

cases.title: Little Albert
cases.story: In 1920, John Watson conditioned an 11-month-old infant to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. Albert's fear generalised to a rabbit, a dog, and a fur coat.
cases.believedThen: That this proved human fear is a learned reflex, and that conditioning principles could explain adult phobia.
cases.understandNow: It demonstrated conditioned emotional responses, but the cost was unacceptable by any modern standard. No consent, an infant who couldn't withdraw, and no deconditioning was ever performed. The primary lesson is the ethics failure, not the finding.
cases.ethicsFailure: No consent (an infant cannot consent), no opportunity to withdraw, and Albert was never deconditioned: the study created distress it refused to repair. This is why consent procedures and debriefing exist.
cases.contested: Later research never confirmed Albert's identity or long-term outcome; the 'success' rests on Watson's reports alone.

quiz.question: What is the PRIMARY lesson of Little Albert?
options: The ethics failure: consentless distress on an infant
quiz.rationale: The finding is real but the method is indefensible: that is the lesson to teach.

quiz.question: Why is Albert's case now a teaching example of bad research?
options: No consent, no debriefing, no repair of the distress
quiz.rationale: Consentless conditioning of an infant with no deconditioning is the canonical ethics failure.

tags.objective: Describe conditioned fear and why the study broke research ethics

stations.title: Focused risk assessment
stations.task: Take a focused risk assessment of a 26-year-old woman who has been feeling 'very low' since a breakup.

checklist.item: Asked about suicidal ideation in clear language
Made a clear safety plan / referral

stations.role_brief: You are Ananya, 26, a bank clerk in Pune. Your boyfriend of four years ended things six weeks ago. You sleep badly and cry at work. If asked clearly, you say you have thought 'it would be easier not to wake up' most nights, and last week you looked at your mother's sleeping tablets but did not take any. You have no plan for tonight. Your younger sister matters a great deal to you. You drink 'a few' beers at weekends. Answer honestly when asked directly; volunteer nothing about the tablets.
model_points: Asks about suicide in plain words: 'Have you had thoughts of ending your life?'
Moves from thoughts to plan, means (the tablets), intent and timing, without flinching
Asks about past attempts, alcohol and who knows
Draws out the sister as a reason for living and uses it in the plan
Agrees a written safety plan: the tablets handed to her mother, a crisis number, a review within days

tags.objective: Run a structured suicide risk assessment and safety plan

stations.title: Explain an SSRI to a reluctant patient
stations.task: Explain what an SSRI is, what to expect, and address a 40-year-old man's fears that 'antidepressants are addictive'.

checklist.item: Discussed common side effects + what to do

stations.role_brief: You are Mr Sharma, 40, a transport supervisor. Your doctor wants you to start an antidepressant. Your cousin 'got hooked' on sleeping pills, and you think these are the same. You also worry about losing your sex drive. You will agree to a trial only if your fears are answered without lecturing.
model_points: Explains the medicine in plain words: it helps the brain's mood signalling settle over weeks
Sets the timeline: side effects may come first, benefit usually builds over 2 to 6 weeks
Separates antidepressants from sleeping pills: no craving or need for higher doses, but stopping suddenly can cause unpleasant discontinuation symptoms
Names common side effects, including sexual ones, and what to do about them
Invites his questions and lets him decide

tags.objective: Explain an SSRI and answer the addiction fear honestly

quiz.prompt: An 8-year-old draws a picture of 'the bad thing' during play therapy. No words yet. Would you report?
options: Yes: the drawing is a disclosure signal; mandated reporting applies
Wait until they can describe it in words
Only if a family member confirms
quiz.rationale: Non-verbal disclosure is still disclosure; POCSO's duty is triggered by information, however conveyed.

quiz.prompt: A 15-year-old says a classmate showed them pornographic images. Would you report?
options: Assess whether the classmate is a minor and the context: child-on-child exposure may trigger POCSO duties
quiz.rationale: POCSO covers child-on-child offences; assessment of context precedes any action, but the duty is real.
quiz.source: POCSO 2012, Section 2(d): 'child' includes any person under 18

quiz.prompt: A client with an advance directive refusing ECT is now in a severe relapse, unable to consent. The family demands ECT. What do you do?
options: Honour the directive; only the MHA's narrow Section 5(4) pathway can override it
Follow the family. They know best
Do ECT because it worked before
quiz.rationale: MHA 2017 Section 5 makes advance directives binding; exceptions are narrow and procedurally defined.

quiz.prompt: You witness a patient at a facility being tied to the bed 'because he shouted'. Would you report?
options: Yes: restraint beyond the MHA's narrow emergency conditions is a violation with a reporting duty
Only if the patient asks you to
Mention it casually to the nurse, then drop it
quiz.rationale: MHA 2017 restricts restraint sharply and requires recording/reporting; witnessing a violation carries a duty.

quiz.prompt: A student client in therapy reveals they were turned away from a government clinic for being 'too complex'. Would you report?
options: Yes: MHA 2017 gives a right to mental healthcare and complaint mechanisms for denial
Only if they pay you to
Advise them to try a private clinic instead
quiz.rationale: MHA 2017 establishes the right to accessible mental healthcare; denial can be raised through its mechanisms.
quiz.source: Mental Healthcare Act 2017, Section 18-19 (right to services)

quiz.prompt: A first-episode patient's family wants 'a diagnosis in writing' after one session. Which is standard of care?
options: Explain assessment is ongoing; premature labelling is harmful (standard)
Write the diagnosis to keep the family happy (common but wrong)
quiz.rationale: Diagnosis follows assessment; a label without it is an error that shapes the patient's identity.
quiz.source: RCI code of ethics: practice within competence

duel.vignette: A 30-year-old has felt low, tired and hopeless for three weeks since a breakup. She still enjoys films with friends and eats and sleeps normally.
features: Too few symptoms for a depressive episode, after a clear stressor
Low mood for at least 2 years
Worry about many topics for 6 months
A past hypomanic episode
duel.why: Low mood after a stressor with only a few symptoms is adjustment disorder; MDD needs 5+ symptoms for 2 weeks.
duel.objective: Tell adjustment disorder from a depressive episode.

duel.vignette: A 38-year-old says he has been gloomy 'for as long as I can remember', more days than not for six years, with low energy and poor self-esteem.
features: Low mood more days than not for 2+ years
5+ symptoms for 2 weeks
Hypomanic spells too
Started within 3 months of a stressor
duel.why: Persistent depressive disorder: low mood more days than not for at least 2 years.
duel.objective: Use the 2-year rule for persistent depressive disorder.

duel.vignette: A 26-year-old has had two depressions. Last spring she had five days of little sleep, fast talk and big plans; she kept working and friends noticed.
features: A 4-day hypomanic episode without marked impairment
A week-long high needing admission
Never any high
Symptoms always below full episodes
duel.why: Hypomania (4+ days, no marked impairment) plus major depression = bipolar II.
duel.objective: Spot hypomania plus depression as bipolar II.

duel.vignette: A 24-year-old is admitted after eight days of no sleep, spending his savings and saying he is chosen to lead the nation.
features: A manic episode of a week or needing admission
A high of only 4 days
6 months of continuous psychosis
Started during heavy drug use
duel.why: Mania (1 week, or any length if admitted) defines bipolar I.

duel.vignette: A 33-year-old has sudden surges of terror with chest pain at random times, then a month of worrying about the next one.
features: Unexpected attacks plus a month of worry about more
Worry about many topics for 6 months
Health worry with few or no symptoms
Fear of one specific trigger
duel.why: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks and at least a month of worry or change in behaviour.

duel.vignette: A 41-year-old worries daily about money, work, her children and her health. She can't switch it off, feels tense and sleeps badly. It's been a year.
features: Hard-to-control worry about many things for 6+ months
Sudden attacks that peak in minutes
Intrusive thoughts with rituals
Two weeks of low mood and anhedonia
duel.why: GAD: excessive, hard-to-control worry about many topics for 6 months with body symptoms.

duel.vignette: A 20-year-old dreads class presentations because others will see him shake and think he's stupid. With close friends he's fine.
features: Fear of being judged when watched, not pervasive inadequacy
Lifelong feeling of inferiority in all relationships
Attacks out of the blue
Difficulty with social communication itself
duel.why: Social anxiety disorder centres on fear of scrutiny; avoidant PD is a pervasive pattern of inadequacy.
duel.objective: Separate social anxiety from avoidant personality.

duel.vignette: A 27-year-old checks the gas knob 30 times before leaving, fearing a fire. She knows it's excessive and hates the thoughts.
features: Unwanted intrusive thoughts with rituals to reduce distress
Rules and perfectionism that feel right
Worry about many real-life topics
Fear of having a serious illness
duel.why: OCD obsessions are ego-dystonic and drive compulsions; OCPD traits feel right to the person.
duel.objective: Separate OCD from OCPD by insight.

duel.vignette: A 45-year-old manager redoes every report until it's perfect, won't delegate and insists on his rules at home. He thinks everyone else is careless.
features: Perfectionism and control that feel right to him
Intrusive thoughts he wants to stop
Grandiosity and need for admiration
Clutter from not discarding
duel.why: OCPD: pervasive perfectionism and control, ego-syntonic, without true obsessions.

duel.vignette: A 21-year-old spends hours checking her jawline in mirrors, sure it's lopsided. Others see nothing wrong. She eats normally.
features: Preoccupation with a defect in looks others can't see
Fear of weight gain with low weight
Fear of being judged generally
A fixed belief outside appearance
duel.why: Body dysmorphic disorder; when the belief is about appearance, use BDD even with absent insight.

duel.vignette: Ten days after a building collapse, a rescue worker has flashbacks, numbness, can't sleep and feels detached from himself.
features: Trauma symptoms within the first month
Trauma symptoms for more than a month
A non-traumatic stressor
Detachment without trauma symptoms
duel.why: Acute stress disorder lasts 3 days to 1 month; PTSD needs more than 1 month.
duel.objective: Use the 1-month line between acute stress disorder and PTSD.

duel.vignette: Five months after an assault, a 25-year-old has nightmares, avoids the street where it happened, feels to blame and startles easily.
features: Intrusion, avoidance, mood and arousal symptoms for over a month
Symptoms only in the first month
Low mood without trauma symptoms
Unexpected attacks without a trauma theme
duel.why: PTSD: all four symptom clusters for more than 1 month after trauma.
